newsitem.title: MEXICO: Future of Mexico drug warrior in doubt after raids.
newsitem.headline: Future of Mexico drug warrior in doubt after raids.

text.p: The future of Mexico's top anti-drug warrior hung in the balance on Tuesday after a newspaper said troops had raided three of his properties and arrested aides on suspicion of protecting drug lords.

Army general Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo was appointed head of the National Institute for the Combat of Drugs (INCD) only last December amid glowing praise from the government and Washington for his exemplary record in fighting traffickers.

Officials said then that the 62-year-old general had a proven record of success in arresting top traffickers and raiding consignments of cocaine and marijuana bound for the United States. But the newspaper Siglo 21 reported on Tuesday that over the weekend the military launched a surprise raid on three of Gutierrez's homes in the western city of Guadalajara and arrested four people.

It quoted unofficial sources as saying the troops were seeking evidence that Gutierrez had protected drug lords, in particular the Arellano Felix brothers, whose cartel operates out of the northern border city of Tijuana.

"The attorney-general's office is in talks with the Defence Ministry about the situation of General Gutierrez Rebollo," an INCD spokeswoman said. "The results of these conversations will be communicated in due course." She declined further comment.

Gutierrez has disappeared from public view since the middle of last week and a Mexico City newspaper said on Monday that he had attempted to commit suicide. But this was denied by the INCD, which said he was recovering from a heart attack in a military hospital.

In Guadalajara, reporters said police were still guarding one of the properties allegedly owned by Gutierrez and raided over the weekend. One local reporter who knew the general well said the Gutierrez affair might not be all it seemed.

The reporter, who asked not to be identified, said he understood from local police sources that the operation might have been an attempt by corrupt generals to topple Gutierrez because of his proven efficiency in hitting drug cartels.
"We think this could be a personal vendetta against the general ... by army members who are protecting drug traffickers," he said.

The confusion surrounding the general was the second drug scandal to erupt in Mexico this week. Over the weekend, two Mexican newspapers published what they said was testimony from witnesses in the United States who alleged that then-President Carlos Salinas de Gortari and his family had partied with a top drug trafficker and benefited from drug money.
Salinas and his jailed brother Raul denied the allegations through their lawyers.
